result.summary: After Tydeus dies, Polynices mourns him and the Thebans fight for his corpse. Hippomedon is lured away by Tisiphone, kills many in the Ismenos, and is drowned and slain after the river god Ismenos grieves for his grandson Crenaeus. Diana tries to save Parthenopaeus, but Mars drives her off and he is mortally wounded by Dryas.

scenes.title: Thebans rage; Polynices hears news
scenes.summary: Thebans are enraged at Tydeus' deed and charge for his body. Fame carries the news to Polynices, who collapses in grief.
scenes.stakes: Polynices stands to lose his most loyal ally and his hope of the throne.

scenes.title: Polynices laments Tydeus
scenes.summary: Polynices mourns over the body, tries to kill himself, and is restrained by friends and Adrastus.
scenes.stakes: Polynices is on the point of suicide.

scenes.title: Hippomedon defends the corpse
scenes.summary: Hippomedon guards Tydeus' body but is tricked by Tisiphone disguised as Halys. The Thebans seize the corpse, and he mounts Tydeus' horse and charges the Thebans.
scenes.stakes: Hippomedon risks losing Tydeus' body and his own life.

scenes.title: Slaughter in the Ismenos
scenes.summary: Hippomedon drives the Thebans into the river and slaughters them, while Hypseus fights back.
scenes.stakes: The Thebans face drowning; Hippomedon is wounded.

scenes.title: Death of Crenaeus; Ismenos' wrath
scenes.summary: The poet explains how Hippomedon killed Crenaeus, the river's grandson. His mother laments and Ismenos complains to Jove.
scenes.stakes: Ismenos' dignity and family are at stake, and Hippomedon will pay.

scenes.title: Death of Hippomedon
scenes.summary: The flooded river overwhelms Hippomedon. Juno pleads with Jove, the waters sink, but Hypseus and Capaneus then kill him on the bank.
scenes.stakes: Hippomedon is fighting for his life against river and army.

scenes.title: Atalanta's dream and prayer
scenes.summary: Parthenopaeus' mother has terrible dreams and prays to Diana. Diana goes to Thebes and meets Apollo, who says fate cannot be changed.
scenes.stakes: Atalanta stands to lose her son.

scenes.title: Parthenopaeus in battle
scenes.summary: Diana arms the boy with deadly arrows. He kills many, and trades taunts with Amphion.
scenes.stakes: Parthenopaeus, young and rash, is set to die in war.

scenes.title: Mars drives off Diana
scenes.summary: Venus rouses Mars, who forces Diana away. Dryas wounds Parthenopaeus, who dies sending a message to his mother.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of the war god; Mavors is another name.

notable_quotes.reason: Capaneus' blasphemous prayer to his own arm, showing his contempt for the gods.
Parthenopaeus' dying message to his mother is among the poem's most moving moments.

analysis.text: The book shows war's escalating savagery and its cost: desecrated corpses, drowned soldiers, and young deaths mourned by parents.
Statius draws on epic tradition, with Homeric similes and gods taking sides, to dramatize the Theban myth for Roman readers of the Flavian age.

fun_facts.text: Statius wrote the Thebaid in the first century AD, and Dante and Chaucer later knew and used it.

language_notes.text: Aonians: Thebans, from Aonia, an old name for Boeotia, the region around Thebes.
Inachidae: the Argives, descendants of Inachus, legendary first king and river-god of Argos.
Tydeus, dying, gnawed the head of his enemy Melanippus, the 'deed' that outrages both sides.
Cadmean: Theban, after Cadmus, the city's founder.
Pelasgians: here a poetic name for the Argives, the enemy.
Hyrcanian tigers and Libyan lions were stock Roman images of wild, man-eating beasts from remote lands.
Oenides: son of Oeneus, i.e. Tydeus.
Greaves are armor for the shins.
"Oenides" means son of Oeneus; Tydeus' father was Oeneus, king of Calydon.
"Emprise" is an archaic word for an enterprise or undertaking, here the war against Thebes.
The "decrees of lot" refer to the agreement that Polynices and Eteocles would rule in alternate years, which Eteocles broke.
"Father of my bride" addresses Adrastus indirectly; Tydeus, though, was Polynices' brother-in-law, so the address is to the grieving circle.
Recalls the night Tydeus and Polynices fought at Adrastus' doorway before the king recognised them as destined sons-in-law.
Telamon and Theseus were heroes of earlier generations; Tydeus' fame is said to eclipse theirs.
"The Father" is Jove; "an I mistake not" means "if I am not mistaken."
Tritonia is Minerva (Athena), and Mavors is Mars; the pairing says the Theban warriors would impress both the goddess and god of war.
Aonian means Theban; Aonia was a region of Boeotia, the area around Thebes.
Ironic sarcasm: the speaker mocks Hippomedon's effort as glorious, calling Tydeus a wild beast who might go home for tears and funeral rites.
Cadmean means Theban, from Cadmus, Thebes' founder; Danaans are the Greeks (Argives).
Sidonian means Phoenician, here loosely Theban, as Cadmus came from Phoenicia.
The Elysian monarch is Pluto, lord of the dead, whom Tydeus' savage deed against Menalippus' head offended; Tisiphone is a Fury acting for him.
Inachian means Argive, from the river Inachus near Argos; Halys is an Argive warrior.
Echionian means Theban, from Echion, one of the Sown Men who founded Thebes.
Sons of Labdacus are the Thebans, named after an early Theban king, grandfather of Oedipus.
"Than of wont" is archaic for "than usual"; the river is swollen beyond its normal flow.
"Spellbound at the warriors" means the waves are held in awe or stilled by the sight of the armed men.
"He too" is Hippomedon, the Argive champion, who plunges in on horseback; the pronoun is unexplained because the preceding lines are omitted.
"Asopian" means descended from or connected with the river Asopus; Hypseus is the son of that river god.
"Targes" are light shields; "casques" are helmets.
"Aetolian charger" is Hippomedon's war horse; "chief" in the same sentence is Hippomedon himself.
Hippomedon refers to the unburied corpse of Tydeus, a hero of the Argive army, whose body Thebes refused to bury; Bellona is the Roman goddess of war.
Caphereus is a dangerous rocky cape on Euboea, famous for shipwrecks, notably of the Greek fleet returning from Troy.
"Doric" here means Greek, specifically Argive; "car" is a chariot.
The learned Sisters are the Muses, daughters of Memory, invoked by epic poets for knowledge of the past.

Grandsire: Crenaeus's grandfather is the river god Ismenos, father of his mother Ismenis. The Elysian Sisters are the Furies' counterparts invoked here as the powers hostile to him; the phrase is obscure.
The stranger from Anthedon is Glaucus, a fisherman turned sea god. Palaemon is the sea god Leucothea's son, who rides a dolphin.
The Sidonian maid is Europa, carried off by Jove as a bull. Her brother Cadmus founded Thebes, hence the Aonian (Theban) race.
Lerna was the marsh where Hercules killed the Hydra; Crenaeus contrasts it with his sacred, undefiled river.
Doris is a sea goddess, mother of the Nereids; her 'brine' means the sea.
Leucothea (Ino) leapt into the sea with her child Palaemon at the Isthmus; she became a sea goddess.
Ismenos recalls Jove's love affairs: Europa as a bull, Alcmena when the night was lengthened, and Semele's death by lightning, a trick of Juno.
The Tirynthian is Hercules; Bromius is Bacchus, whom Ismenos claims to have bathed to quench his burning at birth.
Inachus is the river of Argos, so Hippomedon's homeland; Mycenae stands for the Argive region.
Asopos is a river of the region, here Ismenos' brother; "succour" means help, and "veins" are the river's underground springs.
Setting of the Pleiades and Orion's rising were associated with winter storms at sea, so they stand for tempest.
"Teumesian" means of Teumessus, a hill near Thebes; the river Ismenos is Theban.
The river-god Ismenos is taunted as servant of Bacchus, whose Theban rites were held every third year by frenzied women.
"Tyrians" and later "Phoenician" and "Sidonians" are the Thebans, whose founder Cadmus came from Phoenicia.
Pallas turned against Tydeus after he gnawed his enemy's skull; Delphi is silent because the prophet Amphiaraus was swallowed by the earth.
Refers to Theseus of Athens (Cecrops' city), who forced Thebes to allow burial of the Argive dead after an earlier war.
Capaneus is a notorious despiser of the gods, so he worships his own right arm.
Tegean means from Tegea, an Arcadian city; the 'archer-lad' is Parthenopaeus, and his mother is Atalanta.
Ladon is an Arcadian river. Bathing in running water to wash away the ill effects of a bad dream was a ritual purification.
Lyaeus is Bacchus (Dionysus), 'the loosener'. His Maenads, frenzied women worshippers, wrecking Diana's oak foretells Theban gods threatening her son.
Erymanthian refers to Mount Erymanthus in Arcadia, famed for its boar and bears.
Colchians and Amazons are barbarian peoples; the Amazons were warrior women devoted to Diana-like pursuits, so she claims to outdo them in devotion.
Her 'hated union' and 'fault' allude to her marriage and the birth of her son, a breach of the huntress goddess's virginity ideal.
Dictynna is a title of Diana, linked to nets (hunting nets) and Crete.
'Thy mother's travail and thy brother's splendour' recall Latona's labour in bearing Diana and Apollo, and Apollo's radiance.
Maenalos is a mountain in Arcadia, sacred to Diana and Pan.
The 'engulfed augur' is Amphiaraus, Apollo's prophet, swallowed by the earth in the battle; 'Echionian' means Theban.
Labdacian: Theban, from Labdacus, an ancestor of the Theban royal house. 'Labdacus' sons' in sentence 231 means the Thebans likewise.
Refers to Amphiaraus, Apollo's votary and prophet, swallowed alive by the earth with his chariot at Thebes. Apollo is speaking to his sister Diana.
Niobe boasted of her many children against Latona; Latona's children Apollo and Diana killed them with arrows. Diana is the 'Latonian'.
Oebalian dye: Spartan purple, from Oebalus, a legendary king of Sparta; the term implies fine purple cloth.
Sidonian Nymphs: Theban nymphs, so called because Cadmus, Thebes' founder, came from Sidon in Phoenicia. Teumesus is a hill near Thebes.
Colchian maids: witches of Colchis, home of Medea, famed for magic herbs. Diana is here pictured as patron of such sorcery.
Parrhasian: Arcadian, from Parrhasia, a district of Arcadia, Parthenopaeus' homeland.
Parthenopaeus insults Thebes by recalling Bacchic (Lyaeus is Bacchus) rites, where Theban women were Thyiads, frenzied devotees; Echionian means Theban, from Echion.
Trivia is a name of Diana, goddess of crossroads.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, perhaps meaning 'the marcher'. Venus is Mars's lover; Harmonia, their daughter, married Cadmus, founder of Thebes.
Lato's daughter is Diana, daughter of Latona (Lato). 'Father of the gods' is Jove.
The distaff is spinning gear, women's work. It suggests Diana should keep to her own domain, not war. 'Child' is the poet addressing her.
Ogygian means Theban, from Ogyges, an ancient legendary king associated with Thebes. Mavors is a poetic form of Mars.
Orion, the giant hunter, was killed by Diana (in one tradition), so Dryas inherits hatred of her followers.
Presentiments are forebodings, a sense that something bad is about to happen.
Trivia is a name for Diana, goddess of crossroads.
Aonian means Theban, from Aonia, a region of Boeotia.
The text says Dryas falls and never learns who wounded him; the poet hints the cause will be revealed later.
Lycaeus is a mountain in Arcadia, the homeland of Parthenopaeus and his mother.

context_notes.text: Gradivus is a name for Mars, god of war, who here is repelled by Tydeus' cannibal act.
The king is Eteocles, Polynices' brother, ruling Thebes and leading its defense.
Polynices is the exiled Theban prince whom the Argive army is fighting to restore; Tydeus was his ally and father-in-law's fellow champion.
Polynices calls Tydeus a truer brother because his actual brother Eteocles is his enemy.
Adrastus, king of Argos, had given his daughters to the exiles Polynices and Tydeus, drawing Argos into the war.
Adrastus is Polynices' father-in-law and leader of the Argive army.
Eteocles is the Theban king defending the city against the Argive army led by Polynices and Adrastus.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, avenging goddesses who usually carry torches, scourges and snake hair.
Tydeus came from Aetolia, where the river Achelous flows.
Centaurs were half-man, half-horse creatures; Mount Ossa in Thessaly was associated with them.
The Ismenos is the river near Thebes, sacred in myth and a natural defence on the city's approach.
The Fates were goddesses who spun and cut each person's life-thread, fixing the moment of death.
Diana was the goddess of hunting and chastity; Theron's devotion suggests he was a huntsman.
Crenaeus is a Theban river-grandson, son of Faunus and the nymph Ismenis, daughter of the river Ismenos near Thebes.
Pelasgians here means the Greeks, the Argive besiegers of Thebes led by Hippomedon.
Liber is another name for Bacchus, the Theban-born god of wine.
Ismenos, the river of Thebes, is enraged because Hippomedon has been slaughtering Thebans and choking his stream with corpses.
Juno is patroness of Argos, whose people descend from Inachus, the first river-god and king there.
Jove (Jupiter), Juno's husband, is the Thunderer; his nod signifies assent and commands the waters.
Capaneus is an Argive chief who defies the gods; he will later be struck down by Jove's thunderbolt while scaling Thebes' wall.
Hanging hunting trophies on a sacred tree was a common votive custom, offering the spoils to the deity.
Cadmus founded Thebes, so 'Cadmus' walls' means the city of Thebes.
Parnassus is the mountain near Delphi, sacred to Apollo, Diana's twin brother.
Parthenopaeus is the young Arcadian son of Atalanta, a huntress devoted to Diana, who here pleads for him against fate.
Amphion, a Theban king, was a son of Jove and famed musician who raised Thebes' walls by his lyre.
Venus supports Thebes because her daughter Harmonia married Cadmus, its founder.
Cyllene, Tegea, Aepytus and Telphusa are places in Arcadia, naming Parthenopaeus's troops.

literary_notes.text: The narrator turns directly to Gradivus, heightening the horror: even the war god cannot bear Tydeus' act.
Their anger is compared to what they would feel if their ancestors' graves were desecrated, showing its sacred intensity.
Calling Tydeus' gnawing a 'noble solace of death' is bitter sarcasm from the king.
The Thebans rushing for the corpse are likened to carrion birds darkening the sky, casting them as greedy scavengers.
Fame is a winged messenger who glides into Polynices' ears, making rumor an active, faster-when-evil agent.
His mind and sight being 'whelmed in night' expresses blackout and despair; the falling arms and shield show collapse physically.
Polynices addresses the dead Tydeus directly, opening a lament full of guilt and love.
The blunt, short sentence shows Polynices' guilt and self-blame in his grief.
A run of questions conveys his shock and disorientation as he surveys the many wounds.
Polynices, led away, is compared to a bull that has lost its yoke-mate, conveying numb grief and helpless dependence.
Hippomedon's steadfastness is compared to a rock resisting waves, with even ships recognizing it from afar, conveying immovable strength.
A cow defending her calf from a wolf is likened to Hippomedon guarding the body, emphasizing fierce protectiveness.
The corpse's tug-of-war resembles a ship driven back and forth by a storm despite the helmsman's efforts.
Tisiphone's hair obeys her command and holds its peace, giving her serpent locks a will of their own.
Tydeus, whom Thebans once fled, is now mauled safely by them; the reversal stresses the cruelty of fate.
The dead Tydeus is likened to a slain lion mocked by villagers, showing the Thebans' relief and delight in their former terror.
The horse's charge is likened to a Centaur leaping down Ossa, magnifying his wild force.
The swollen river is called an omen of disaster, anticipating the slaughter that follows.
Hippomedon is compared to a dolphin scattering terrified fish, making the Thebans seem helpless prey.
Severed heads and arms floating to rejoin bodies is a grotesque, exaggerated image of the carnage.
The dismembered Argipus looks at his own arms in the branches, a macabre image of the war's horror.
Agenor's loyalty to his brother, which drowns him, stirs pity amid the carnage.
The poet's exclamation, "Behold the power of fate!", directly addresses the reader and stresses irony: a sailor dies in a river.
The river is treated as a kindly grandfather, supporting the boy's steps and flowing backward for him.
Crenaeus's ease on the water is compared to sea gods Glaucus, Triton and Palaemon.
The description of the engraved shield pauses the action; the bull seems to move, blurring art and reality.
The cut-off cry of 'Mother!' and the water choking his voice make the death piteous.
Mourning Nymph is compared to Alcyone, the kingfisher, whose nest is wrecked by storm.
Reigning in the flood bitterly contrasts with his dead body; the river's ruler has fallen.
She addresses the absent Ismenos, accusing him of sluggishness while his enemy boasts.
Ismenos is a majestic aged god with moss-grown neck and icy hair, rising from his cavern.
The swelling river is compared to a storm-tossed sea, enlarging the combat to cosmic scale.
The river is a furious god fighting a man, and the shield splits the stream as a weapon would.
The ash offering help becomes the instrument of his ruin, as it collapses and dams the water around him.
Hippomedon's fall is likened to a huge oak on Haemus, stressing his grandeur and the awe of onlookers.
Capaneus' prayer to his own arm is answered at once by himself, expressing his impious self-reliance.
The dying hero is compared to a besieged tower collapsing, opening the city, and echoing the war's theme.
The dreams of fallen spoils, a son's armour returning without him, and burning images foretell Parthenopaeus' death.
Steel gleaming among green shade vividly pictures the crowded tree of trophies, merging weapons with nature.
Atalanta addresses the goddess directly, pleading with a catalogue of her devotion to win favour.
She begs to die first, yet the prayer is ineffective; the goddess cannot alter fate, so her wish for mercy is unfulfilled.
The marble statue weeping suggests the goddess's sympathy and the grim omen, nature and image sharing human grief.
The red glow and clashing bows and quivers show the twin gods' meeting in grand, cosmic terms.
The lavish hunting finery presents Parthenopaeus as a beautiful, untried youth playing at war, preparing for his pathos.
The lion cub breaking free of its den compares the boy's reckless eagerness to an animal outgrowing its mother's protection.
The narrator suddenly addresses the boy, heightening the drama of his killing spree.
Sword and bow set against hollow drums contrasts Arcadian martial manliness with supposed Theban effeminacy.
Diana smiles through tears, knowing the boy's boasts of trophies are doomed; mixed emotion foreshadows his death.
Anger accompanies Mars and the Madnesses are busy in battle, treating abstract passions as divine attendants.
The swan facing the eagle with thunderbolt compares Parthenopaeus's terror before Dryas, making the boy seem small and prey-like.
Exclamations of pity for his youth and the purple blood on white skin heighten sorrow for the dying boy.
Even dying, he thinks of his mother's feelings and takes the blame, showing tender, dutiful character.
